name: Adenoidectomy for facial growth

card.summary: Surgical removal of enlarged adenoids in children to restore nasal breathing, which some people link to healthier jaw and face development.
card.note: A medical surgery under general anesthesia, decided by an ENT specialist; indications are set by airway and ear problems.

quick.overview:
Adenoidectomy is the surgical removal of the adenoids, a pad of lymphoid tissue at the back of the nose. In children, enlarged adenoids can block the nose and push breathing to the mouth. Looksmaxxing discussion connects chronic mouth breathing with a longer, narrower face and dental changes, so restoring nasal breathing is seen as a way to support better facial development.
Clinically, the operation is performed for obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, persistent middle-ear fluid and recurrent ear infections. Orthodontic and ENT writers describe a link between mouth breathing and facial form, and the clinical picture of an open-mouth, long-face look is called adenoid facies. Trials of adenoidectomy are mostly designed around breathing, sleep and ear outcomes rather than face shape.
quick.how: The procedure is an outpatient operation under general anesthesia, usually lasting about half an hour, often in early childhood when adenoids are largest. Families reach it through a pediatrician or ENT specialist after symptoms such as snoring, mouth breathing, or ear fluid. Recovery is typically one to two weeks with soft foods and reduced activity.
quick.risks: Reported complications are uncommon and include bleeding, infection, temporary or rare lasting speech changes (velopharyngeal insufficiency) and regrowth of adenoid tissue. Anesthesia carries its own risks in children. Adenoids shrink naturally by adolescence, and surgery is mainly a childhood and specialist decision; adults seldom need it.

lead: Adenoidectomy is the surgical removal of the adenoids, lymphoid tissue in the nasopharynx behind the nose that is largest in early childhood and usually shrinks after puberty.[1][2] It is among the most common pediatric operations, often performed together with tonsillectomy.[3]

In looksmaxxing discussion, adenoidectomy appears as a way to help facial development: when enlarged adenoids obstruct the nose, a child may breathe through the mouth, and orthodontic and ENT literature associates long-term mouth breathing with a longer, narrower face and dental changes.[4] Restoring nasal breathing early is therefore described as a route to a more favourable growth pattern.

Medical practice performs the operation for breathing and ear indications rather than for appearance. Guidelines cite obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, otitis media with effusion lasting more than three months, and recurrent ear infections as the main reasons.[1][3] The clinical look of open mouth and long face associated with adenoid hypertrophy is called adenoid facies.[5]

chain: Nasal breathing supports typical jaw and facial development in growing children
angle.text: Proponents see adenoidectomy as a way to remove a physical airway block during the years the face is growing, so that nasal breathing and mouth posture can follow a typical pattern. The operation is done in childhood for breathing and ear reasons, and any facial benefit is described as a downstream effect of better airflow.

paras: The adenoids form part of Waldeyer's ring, a ring of lymphoid tissue in the throat. They grow from birth, peak at roughly six to eight years of age and usually atrophy after puberty.[2] The operation removes this tissue through the mouth under general anesthesia using curettage, suction diathermy, microdebrider, coblation or other techniques.[2][6]

Adenoid hypertrophy is common in children aged two to seven and is linked to recurrent upper-airway infection, allergy and smoke exposure.[2][5] Enlarged adenoids can cause nasal obstruction, snoring and hyponasal speech.

Current guidance lists obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, persistent middle-ear effusion and recurrent acute otitis media as the principal indications, with chronic rhinosinusitis less often.[1][3][7] Pediatric reviews note that most tonsil and adenoid surgery is now performed for obstructive symptoms rather than infection.[3]

Wikipedia notes that the operation's history includes now-abandoned uses, such as for general health promotion, and that use declined from the 1930s as trials showed limited benefit for several indications.[1][8]

Chronic mouth breathing in children has been proposed to contribute to a long, narrow face and dental changes, sometimes called long face syndrome, though the relationship may run in both directions: a narrow airway may predispose to mouth breathing.[4] Adenoid facies describes the open-mouth appearance associated with adenoid hypertrophy and is considered a clinical finding rather than a disease.[5]

Orthodontic and ENT discussion of this theme concerns children whose faces are still growing. The reported appeal for looks-focused readers is that removing the obstruction is the one surgical step that directly restores the nasal route.

Recovery generally takes one to two weeks, with throat discomfort, nasal stuffiness and bad breath.[6] Reported complications include postoperative bleeding in roughly 0.5 to 2 percent of cases, infection, rarely velopharyngeal insufficiency affecting speech, and regrowth requiring revision.[6] Perioperative respiratory events and emergence delirium in children are studied topics in pediatric anesthesia.[9][10]

Randomized and other trials of adenoidectomy have mainly measured sleep-disordered breathing, ear outcomes, surgical technique and anesthesia recovery. A review of otitis media notes ventilation tubes and adenoid surgery as options for persistent effusion.[11] Guidelines for tympanostomy tubes and tonsillectomy set out patient selection and indications.[7][12] Registered trials compare surgical methods such as coblation, microdebrider and partial versus total removal; one registered trial lists growth among its conditions.[13][14] No published trial identified measured facial skeletal outcomes as its primary endpoint.

timeline.event: Wilhelm Meyer first performs adenoid removal, using ring forceps through the nose.[8]
Use declines as antimicrobials and trials limit indications.[8]
AAO-HNS publishes a pediatric tonsillectomy guideline; updated in 2019.[12]

lore.intro: Facial-growth discussion in looksmaxxing circles tends to link nasal breathing to jaw and mid-face development, with adenoidectomy mentioned as the surgical way to clear a blocked airway in childhood.

claims.claim: Mouth breathing in childhood leads to a longer, narrower face
claims.believers: Proponents point to the adenoid facies look and to orthodontic writing on long face syndrome.[5]
claims.experts: Clinical sources describe the association and note the relationship may run in both directions.[4]

claims.claim: Removing adenoids early can steer facial growth toward a more typical pattern
claims.believers: Advocates reason that restored nasal breathing removes the driver of open-mouth posture.
claims.experts: Adenoidectomy is indicated for breathing and ear conditions; no trial in the sources measured facial skeletal change as its main outcome.[1][3]
